Mental rotation of objects and scenes

Between 9 and 12 years of age, children’s mental rotation of both objects and scenes becomes faster, more accurate, and more automatic, pushing their spatial transformations closer to an adult-like regime. For object-based tasks, one recent study using 3D cube aggregates (i.e 4-6 connected colored cubes) found roughly 10% higher mental-rotation accuracy in 10-11-year-olds than in 8-9-year-olds, suggesting a meaningful boost in how efficiently children can encode, chunk, and transform multi-part configurations in working memory 1. Over the same age range, scene rotation (perspective-taking) tasks show parallel improvements: when asked to imagine another person’s viewpoint across a range of angular disparities, 12-year-olds produce faster, more reliable judgments about what the other person sees and how left-right relations change with viewpoint, reflecting a growing ability to use genuine mental rotation of the whole scene (rather than ad hoc visual matching or rule-based guessing) to solve these problems 2, 3. Overall, these trends suggest that between 9 and 12, children’s overall spatial cognitive repertoire consolidates into a more unified, high-capacity "3D workspace" in which objects and viewpoints can be rapidly and flexibly transformed, supporting more sophisticated navigation, tool use, and social perspective taking.

Navigation and cognitive mapping

By 9 years of age, children possess a rudimentary cognitive map that lets them handle large-scale spaces, identify shortcuts using metric information, and switch between egocentric and allocentric reference frames; between 9 and 12, navigation performance on top of this scaffold improves rapidly and mostly smoothly rather than via sharp qualitative jumps. Across this window, the quantity and quality of landmarks and directions that children can produce and recognize in both verbal and visuospatial tasks increase, they more reliably select decisional landmarks (those at choice points), and they become better at binding landmarks to the directions that follow them 4. They also show higher accuracy in learning a new environment after a single exposure, particularly in large virtual environments 5, and they more spontaneously switch between egocentric and allocentric strategies rather than sticking rigidly to a single frame of reference 6, 7. Exploration becomes faster and more efficient across a variety of environments 8, 6, 9, while susceptibility to confusion under rotations or rearrangements of landmarks and other navigational cues decreases, indicating more stable underlying spatial reference frames 10, 11. Children's cognitive maps combine landmarks and routes. (Figure). Children use both egocentric and allocentric representations. (Figure).

By around 12 years, several studies indicate that overall navigation performance is broadly similar to adults but still noticeably slower and more error prone 12, 13. For instance, in large-scale virtual navigation tasks, 12-year-olds can reach adult levels of performance 14, 15, and can even be categorized into the same three adult-like groups: imprecise navigators (who form only imprecise ideas of routes), non-integrators (who represent routes more accurately but are imprecise in relating two routes), and integrators (who relate the two routes and, thus, form cognitive maps) 15. At the level of cue integration and environmental structure, 10-11-year-olds are already near-optimal in combining visual and self-motion information when reproducing a walked path, especially under challenging conditions such as darkness 16, and by 11 they can "regularize" irregular environments whose layout must be inferred from the inclination and angle of maze walls, matching adult performance 17.

Overall, these findings suggest that 12-year-olds operate with a fast, flexibly updatable, near-adult cognitive map in which landmarks, routes, metrics, and multiple reference frames are tightly integrated, meaning that their world model for large-scale space has become a richly structured, inferential map that can support efficient navigation and planning in complex environments. Essentially, these children are "zooming out" and beginning to abstract from their immediate environments to derive efficient, reusable strategies for long-horizon tasks; one way this is apparent in the spatial domain is in the more-rapid advancement of extrinsic (between-object relationships) spatial cognition relative to intrinsic (within-object relationships) during this window 18.
